Saturday, 12 April 2031. Isabelle has emptied the cellar of her Paris flat and found her father’s old trunk. Inside were his logbooks, from 1962 to 1985. She has come to Lyon to show them to Odile. They read together in the sitting room on rue d’Austerlitz.
Listen, Mum. The first notebook starts in November 1962. “On 14 November, I went aboard the Ville-de-Marseille. The ship weighed anchor at dawn.”
He always wrote in the passé simple in his notebooks. Like in novels. He said life at sea deserved the passé simple.
“I stayed on deck a long time. Lyon was far away. I thought of her all night. I did not write to her. I did not have the courage.”
“Of her.” He’s talking about Hélène. He had just come back from Algeria, with his hand. He left without saying goodbye to her.
There are whole pages about her, for years. And then, in 1971… listen: “On 3 June, we dropped anchor at Marseille. When I had finished my watch, I went ashore.”
(turns pale) 3 June 1971. That’s the day we met.
“In a café on the Vieux-Port, I saw a young woman laughing with her friends. She had a laugh that drowned out the noise of the harbour. I could not stop myself looking at her.”
That was me. I was twenty-one. I was a medical student. I laughed a lot in those days.
“She came over to me and asked me for a light. I had none. I did not smoke. She laughed again. It was the first time since Lyon that I laughed too.”
(tears in her eyes) He never told me that. Never. In fifty years he never told me I had been the first to make him laugh.
He wrote it. Maybe that’s why he wrote in the passé simple. What you can’t say out loud, you write like a story.
Read me the rest, darling. Slowly. I’ve waited sixty years to hear this.

The passé simple is the past tense of WRITTEN NARRATIVE: novels, fairy tales, biographies, history articles. In speech it’s hardly used at all; the passé composé replaces it. At B2 you mainly need to RECOGNISE and understand it.
English uses one simple past (“he left”) for both. Think of the passé simple as the “storybook” past and the passé composé as the “conversation” past.
In texts you’ll meet almost only the third person (il, elle, ils, elles). Focus on: -a / -èrent (-er verbs), -it / -irent, -ut / -urent.

Trap: some forms look like the present. “Il dit” can be present OR passé simple (dire). “Il vit” can be the passé simple of voir (he saw) OR the present of vivre (he lives). “Il fit” (passé simple of faire) ≠ “il fait” (present). Context decides.

Passé antérieur = the auxiliary in the PASSÉ SIMPLE + the participle. It shows an action completed just before another, in a passé simple narrative. It appears after quand, dès que, lorsque, après que, aussitôt que:
When I had finished my watch, I went ashore.
As soon as she had left, he opened the letter.
After they had eaten, they went up on deck.
It’s the literary equivalent of the pluperfect for a quick sequence. In speech: “Quand j’ai eu fini…” or simply “Après avoir fini…”.

Lyon was far away (setting). I thought of her all night (action).
She was laughing with her friends (setting). She came over to me (action).

At the beginning of April, Isabelle had made a big decision. She was going to leave Paris. She was fifty-seven, she had worked from home for her publishing house since the pandemic, and nothing kept her in the capital any more. Her mother was eighty, with repeated bouts of bronchitis and a walking stick. Isabelle wanted to live near her, while there was still time.

Before selling her flat in Montmartre, she had to empty the cellar. She hadn’t been down there for years. There were boxes of books, old furniture, toys from her childhood and, right at the back, behind a rusty bicycle, a dark wooden trunk fastened with two leather straps. On the lid, two letters had been carved with a knife: “H. B.”

It was her father’s sea chest. She vaguely remembered seeing it in her parents’ attic when she was little. After Henri’s death, her mother had asked her to keep it, because she didn’t have the strength to open it. Isabelle had taken it down to her cellar and forgotten it. For eight years.

She undid the straps, sitting on the floor in the dust, under a bare bulb. Inside were an old sailor’s pea jacket, a brass compass, a pipe Henri had never smoked and, carefully stacked, twenty-three little black notebooks, numbered one to twenty-three. On the first one it said: “Logbook, 1962”. On the last: “1985”.

Isabelle opened the first notebook at random. Her father’s handwriting, slanting and cramped, filled every page. She read a sentence, then two, then a whole page. She only realised she was crying when a tear fell on the ink. She closed the notebook very quickly, as if she had been caught reading someone else’s mail.

She didn’t go on. These notebooks, she thought, weren’t hers. They belonged first to her mother. The following Saturday she took the TGV to Lyon with the twenty-three notebooks in a travel bag, clutched to her for two hours, as Odile had clutched the Marseille lime tree on her lap.

Odile looked at the notebooks for a long time without touching them. She knew Henri kept a diary at sea; she had seen him write thousands of times, in the evening, at the kitchen table. But she had never read them. “They were his,” she said. “A sailor has the right to have secrets.” Then she asked her daughter to read her the first one. Aloud. Her eyes could no longer read Henri’s cramped writing.

That was how the Saturday readings began. Every week, Isabelle came from Paris, sat on the stool next to her mother’s armchair and read a notebook. Ioana and Julien sometimes came to listen, with the children. Henri-Ion always fell asleep after ten minutes, lulled by Isabelle’s voice and his namesake’s passé simple.

For Henri had written all his notebooks in the passé simple. Not a single passé composé in twenty-three years. “The ship weighed anchor at dawn.” “We weathered a storm off the Cape.” “I thought of her all night.” Julien, listening, felt he was hearing an adventure novel. Odile smiled. “He said life at sea deserved the passé simple,” she explained. “And that life on land made do with the passé composé.”

The first notebooks spoke almost only of Hélène. Henri never named her. He wrote “her”, always in italics, underlined twice. He described the sleepless nights, the shame of his mutilated hand, the letters he began and never finished. Isabelle read slowly, glancing at her mother from time to time to check she could go on.

Odile listened without flinching. She knew the story. Four years earlier, she had given Hélène the letter of 3 May 1963 that Henri had never sent. But hearing her husband’s voice, at twenty-three, declaring his love for another woman was something else. She only said, at the end of the second notebook: “Poor boy. He was so alone.”

In the third notebook was the page for 3 May 1963. Isabelle read it in a trembling voice: Henri on deck, off Gibraltar, playing the waltz on the harmonica for Hélène’s birthday; the letter written in the night, the envelope sealed, the stamp; and, at dawn, the decision not to send it. And then the promise: every 3 May, wherever he was, he would whistle the waltz.

“He kept it, his promise,” Odile murmured. “Every 3 May, for fifty years. I didn’t know why. He said it was an old sailor’s habit. I believed him until the day Julien found the score in the piano.” Rose-Hélène, sitting on the floor with her harmonica, looked up. “I whistle on 3 May too,” she announced. It wasn’t true. But it would become true.

The following notebooks were about the sea. The ports of Africa and South America, the storms off the Cape of Good Hope, the starry nights of the Indian Ocean. Yves Le Goff appeared often, always cooking or telling Breton stories. Hélène came back less and less often. The name in italics gradually disappeared from the pages, like a coast you leave behind.

One passage made everyone laugh. In 1968, off Brazil, Yves Le Goff had wanted to make Breton crêpes for the captain’s birthday. For lack of buckwheat flour, he used cassava flour bought in a port. “The crêpes were inedible,” Henri wrote. “The captain ate them anyway, out of politeness. He was ill for two days. Yves swore he would never cook again. He started again the next day.”

Odile asked for a copy of this passage to send to Yves in Nantes. He replied by return of post, in a shaky hand: “It wasn’t the cassava. It was the rum. But don’t tell anyone.” Odile laughed for five minutes, a laugh nobody had heard from her in months. Julien thought that that laugh, the one from the café on the Vieux-Port, had never really disappeared.

Then came notebook number nine. 1971. Isabelle opened it one Saturday in April, at four in the afternoon. She read the entry for 3 June: the stopover in Marseille, the watch finished, going ashore, the café on the Vieux-Port, the young woman laughing with her friends whose laugh drowned out the noise of the harbour. Odile turned pale. Then she asked her daughter to go on.

“She came over to me and asked me for a light. I had none. She laughed again. It was the first time since Lyon that I laughed too.” Odile closed her eyes. In fifty years, Henri had never told her that. He had never told her that she had been the first, after nine years of silence, to make him laugh.

The rest of the notebook described the following weeks. Henri had extended his stopover. He saw the young woman again the next day, then the day after. Her name was Odile. She was a medical student. On the fourth day she asked him what was wrong with his left hand, which he always hid in his pocket. Nobody had ever asked him so directly.

Isabelle read the next page, stopping at every sentence. “She took my hand in hers. She looked at it for a long time, without pity and without disgust, the way a doctor looks at a wound. Then she said: ‘It must have hurt you very much.’ No one had ever said that to me. I wept in front of her, in the middle of the café. She did not let go of my hand.”

In the sitting room on rue d’Austerlitz, nobody spoke. Julien was watching Odile. Ioana was holding Rose-Hélène’s hand. Isabelle had put the notebook down on her knees. Odile, eyes closed, was smiling. “I remember,” she said at last. “I remember his hand. He was ashamed of it. I thought it was beautiful. It was the hand of a man who had survived.”

Rose-Hélène, who didn’t understand everything, tugged at her mother’s sleeve. “Mummy, what’s the passé simple?” Ioana thought. How do you explain that to a three-year-old? “It’s the tense of stories,” she finally answered. “The tense you use to tell the things that really matter.” Rose-Hélène nodded, very serious, as if she had understood perfectly.

On the following Saturdays they read about the wedding, in 1972, in a little church in Marseille; Isabelle’s birth, in 1974, told over four pages full of spelling mistakes, because Henri, that day, was too moved to reread himself; the long absences, the returns, the quarrels and reconciliations. Isabelle discovered a father she hadn’t known: funny, anxious, tender, clumsy.

“My daughter was born this morning at six,” he had written. “She weighed three kilos. She cried very loudly, like her mother when she laughs. I took her in my arms with my injured hand, and for the first time since Algeria, I was not ashamed of that hand.” Isabelle had to stop reading. Odile took the notebook from her hands and held it to her chest.

In the 1980 notebook there was a page Isabelle couldn’t manage to read to the end. Henri described a stopover in Marseille, the summer she was six. She had sung to him, on the terrace of their little house, a song she had learned at school. “She sang out of tune,” Henri had written. “She sang out of tune and very loudly, with all her heart. I understood that evening that I had nothing to teach her. She already knew everything that matters.”

Isabelle closed the notebook and went out onto the landing, so nobody would see her cry. Ioana followed her. The two of them stayed there, sitting on the first step of the stairs, for ten minutes. “I thought he never listened to me,” Isabelle said at last. “He was always somewhere else, always at sea, even when he was at home. In fact, he listened to everything. He wrote everything down.”

Julien asked permission to read a few pages to the La Duchère children. Odile agreed, on condition that he chose the passages himself. The following Wednesday, Théo read the page for 3 May 1963 to the orchestra, the one with the deck, the harmonica and the letter never sent. The children listened without moving. Then Yanis raised his hand.

“Sir, why didn’t he send the letter?” Julien thought for a long time. “Because he was afraid,” he answered. “Afraid she had forgotten him. And afraid she hadn’t.” Yanis frowned. “But that’s stupid. He should have sent it.” Inès, beside him, sighed. “Obviously it’s stupid. Otherwise there wouldn’t have been a waltz.”

On the last Saturday in April, Isabelle opened notebook number twenty-three. 1985. Henri’s last year at sea. He was forty-five. He had decided to stay ashore, to see his daughter grow up; she was eleven. The last pages told of the last voyage, from Dakar to Marseille, and the last night on deck.

“Tonight I went up on deck for the last time. The sea was calm. I played the waltz on the harmonica, as every night for twenty-three years. Then I took a last look at the stars. Tomorrow I go home to land. I have a wife who laughs and a daughter who sings. I think I have finished waiting.”

Isabelle noticed that for the last sentence her father had abandoned the passé simple. “Tomorrow I go home. I have a wife. I have finished waiting.” The present. The passé composé. The tense of the land, as he used to say. The tense of those who no longer leave. When Isabelle pointed it out to her, Odile simply nodded. She had understood it before her.

As she closed the last notebook, Isabelle felt something slip between the pages and fall onto her knees. It was a small dried flower, yellowed and very fragile, pressed in a piece of tissue paper. On the paper, in a handwriting much younger than that of the notebooks, it read: “Lime blossom. Parc de la Tête d’Or. 3 May 1962.”

Nobody dared touch the flower. It had travelled for twenty-three years in a sailor’s notebooks, across all the seas of the world, then slept for eight years in a cellar in Montmartre. It was a flower from the tree under which Henri and Hélène had kissed for the first time. The tree whose twelve little lime trees were, at that very moment, being planted all over France.

The following Monday, Julien took the flower to Mr Fournier, in his greenhouse, wrapped in three layers of tissue paper. The old gardener examined it for a long time with a magnifying glass, without touching it. Then he looked up. “It’s definitely a flower from our tree,” he said. “The shape of the bract doesn’t lie. It used to flower earlier in those days. The climate has changed. It hasn’t.”

At the office, Amina asked for permission to digitise the twenty-three notebooks, page by page, for the network’s archives. Odile agreed, on condition that nobody read them before Isabelle’s death. “A sailor’s secrets stay in the family,” she said. “The children have a right to the waltz. Not to the rest.” Amina noted the condition in a spreadsheet, in red. Then she spent three weeks scanning the notebooks, one by one, without reading a single line.

Odile asked for the flower to be framed and hung in the Hélène Morel hall, next to the photo of Henri as a sailor and the one of Hélène on her bench. “That way,” she said, “the three of them will finally be together: her, him, and their tree.” For the notebooks she made another decision. They would go to Rose-Hélène, on her twentieth birthday, with the score, the cassette and the rest.

That evening, before going back to Paris, Isabelle announced the news she had been keeping for three weeks. She had found a flat in Lyon, on rue des Fantasques, five minutes from rue d’Austerlitz, with a view of the Rhône. She would move in July. Odile looked at her for a long time. Then she said, in a voice that trembled a little: “Your father would be pleased. He always said families should live by the same sea.”

Henri-Ion, for his part, discovered laughter during those Saturday readings. He was almost four months old. One afternoon, while Isabelle was reading a passage about a storm, Rose-Hélène imitated the sound of the wind by blowing into the harmonica, very loudly, right next to him. He burst out laughing. It was his first real laugh, a baby’s laugh, high-pitched and unexpected. The whole room stopped to listen.

Odile looked at the baby laughing in his mother’s arms. “He laughs like him,” she said softly. “Henri laughed exactly like that, with his whole face, when he was surprised.” Nobody dared point out that a four-month-old baby couldn’t look like a man who wasn’t from his family. In that flat, anyway, nobody really believed in coincidences any more.

Later, when everyone had gone, Odile opened her own little notebook, the one in which she usually noted Mr Fournier’s advice about the lime trees. On a blank page, in her large slanting hand, she wrote a single sentence. She showed it to nobody. But Julien saw it a few weeks later, while looking for a note about watering.

The sentence was written in the passé simple, the tense of stories, the tense of sailors. “On 26 April 2031, I learned at last that I had been the first to make him laugh.” And underneath, in the present, as if to come home to land herself: “I am no longer waiting for anything. I have everything.”

Reading text: A page from the diary
Here is a page from Henri’s logbook, written in 1963. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
3 May 1963. Calm sea. We sailed along the coast of Spain all day. The sun set over Gibraltar around nine. It was her birthday. She was twenty-one.
When I had finished my watch, I went up on deck. There was no one. I took the harmonica out of my pocket and played the waltz. I played it badly, with my injured hand. But I played it to the end.
Later I went down to my cabin and wrote a letter. I told her everything: Algeria, the hand, the shame. I told her I still loved her. I asked her forgiveness for not coming back.
I put the letter in an envelope. I wrote her address, at Fourvière. I stuck on the stamp. Then I kept it on my chest until morning. At dawn, I did not send it.
I do not know why. Perhaps because I believed she had forgotten me. Perhaps because I was afraid she had not forgotten me. I put the letter away at the bottom of my bag. It stayed there.
Tonight I made a promise. Every 3 May, wherever I am, I will whistle the waltz. She will not hear it. But I will know that I have not forgotten her. It is all I can do. It is very little.
